Yakṣagāna
------------------------------------------
One of the best means of spreading religion—as spiritual evolution and ethical values—among the masses is through properly designed dramas with appropriate मुसिच् and dance. Folk dramas with religious themes, taken mostly from the epics and the पुराणस्, have been serving this purpose for centuries.
The Kathakkaḷī of the Kerala State and the यक्षगान prevalent in the Karnataka State are two such arts worth mentioning. (See KATHAKKAḶĪ for details.)
Though based on the techniques given in the Nāṭyaśāstra of भरत, the यक्षगान has attained a strong local colour. The artists not only dance vigorously but also sing and talk according to the roles they have to play. There is enough scope to show their talents through impromptu speeches also. The stories and themes are taken mostly from the epics and the पुराणस्.
At the background is the master who narrates the story and also sings to the accompaniment of simple musical instruments. Now-a-days use of the harmonium and the mṛdaṅga (drum) has become quite common. So also the modern stage set-up.
As far as the costumes and make-up of the artists are concerned, they are very similar to the ones used in the Kathakkaḷī.
Over the years three different traditions of यक्षगान have evolved due to local variations.

Yakṣa
------------------------------------------
Though the word यक्ष occurs in the Ṛgveda several times (1.190.4; 4.3.13 etc.) its meaning is not clear. Traditional commentators interpret it as a feast or sacrifice. The word occurring in the Atharvaveda (8.9.25) is sometimes interpreted as a monster.
In the Kena Upaniṣad (3) ब्रह्मन् is said to have assumed the form of a यक्ष to test the gods.
In the epics and the पुराणस् the yakṣas are described as semi-divine beings along with विद्याधरस्, गन्धर्वस् and किन्नरस्. They were the offsprings of Kāśyapa and Khasā (vide Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.21.25).
Kubera, the god of wealth, is the lord of the yakṣas.

Yakṣapraśna
(‘questions [raised by the] यक्ष’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the most important sections of the great epic Mahābhārata (Vanaparva or Araṇyaparva 313). It comprises 90 verses (from 45 up to 134) and is in the form of a long dialogue between यम (the god of death) disguised as a यक्ष (a demigod) and युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas. The यक्ष asks 122 questions and युधिष्ठिर answers all of them satisfactorily.
After losing in the game of dice, the Pāṇḍavas had to live in a forest for twelve years. Once, during this period of banishment, a ब्राह्मण complained to them that a deer had accidentally carried away his araṇis (wooden pieces used for attrition to generate the Vedic fire). All the five Pāṇḍavas tried their best to pursue the animal and catch it or kill it but failed miserably. When they were resting under a tree, tired and thirsty, युधिष्ठिर sent नकुल to fetch some drinking water. As he did not return even after a long time, the other three brothers were also sent one by one. When none of them turned up, युधिष्ठिर himself went in search of them. To his great astonishment and shock, he found all of them lying dead by the side of a beautiful lake. As he was reflecting in himself how it could happen, he saw a यक्ष of gigantic proportions. The यक्ष told him that his brothers had died since they did not heed not to drink the water of the lake that really belonged to him, unless they answered his questions. युधिष्ठिर in all humility did obeisance to him and offered to answer his queries to the best of his ability. Then ensued a long series of enigmatic questions and scintillating answers.
Many of the questions are like riddles. The answers given by Yudhiṣṭhira—in spite of the explanations offered by नीलकण्ठ चतुर्धर (A. D. 1400) in his commentary Bhāvārthadīpikā—are also enigmatic. Hence, only a brief summary of the dialogue which is more intelligible and appears convincing, can now be given:
Yakṣa—How does a person become a श्रोत्रिय or a Vedic scholar? By what means does he attain महत् or the Great? What is it that helps a man in difficulties? How does a person become wise?
Yudhiṣṭhira—A person becomes a श्रोत्रिय or Vedic scholar by studying and understanding the spirit of the वेदस्. It is by तपस् or austerity that one can attain महत् or God. It is dhṛti or inner strength that helps a man in difficulties. A person becomes wise by serving the elders and superiors.
*
Yakṣa—How can ब्राह्मणस् attain devatva or godliness? What is the धर्म or the conduct that makes them good? What is the common nature of human beings? By what do they become bad?
Yudhiṣṭhira—Brāhmaṇas attain devatva or godliness by a deep study of the वेदस्. The धर्म that makes them good is तपस् or austerity. It is death that is common to all human beings. They become bad by slander.
*
Yakṣa—By what do the kṣattriyas attain devatva? What is the virtue that makes them good? What constitutes their humanness? By what do they become bad?
Yudhiṣṭhira—It is military prowess that makes the kṣattriyas excellent. It is यज्ञ or performance of sacrifices—that is the virtue they have to cultivate. It is fear that constitutes their humanness. They become bad by abandoning those that seek refuge.
*
Yakṣa—What is it that is heavier or greater than the earth? What is it that is higher than the sky? What is it that is swifter than the wind? What is more numerous than grass?
Yudhiṣṭhira—It is one’s मोथेर् that is greater than the earth. It is one’s ड़थेर् who is higher than the sky. It is the मिन्द् that is swifter than the wind. It is worries that are more numerous than grass.
*
Yakṣa—What are the sources of धर्म (righteousness), yaśas (fame), स्वर्ग (heaven) and sukha (happiness)?
Yudhiṣṭhira—Dākṣya or integrity is the source of धर्म. दान or charity is the source of yaśas. It is सत्य or truth alone that is the source of हेअवेन्. And, it is śīla or character that is the source of happiness.
*
Yakṣa—What is the best means of dhana or wealth? Which is the best wealth? Which is the best lābha or gain? Which is the best sukha or happiness?
Yudhiṣṭhira—It is dākṣya or integrity that is the best means of wealth. It is śruta or learning that is the best wealth. Ārogya or good health is the best gain. तुष्टि or contentment is the best happiness.
*
Yakṣa—By renouncing which does one become lovable? By renouncing which does one become free from grief? By renouncing which does one become wealthy? By renouncing which does one become happy?
Yudhiṣṭhira—One becomes lovable by renouncing pride. One becomes free from grief by renouncing anger. One becomes wealthy by renouncing desire. One becomes happy by renouncing greed.
*
Yakṣa—What is the greatest wonder in this world?
Yudhiṣṭhira—Seeing that every day beings are dying, others who are still living think that they never die. What can be more wonderful than this?
Yakṣa—Then, what is the way?
Yudhiṣṭhira—Disputations take us nowhere. Scriptures teach mutually contradictory things. No single sage has been accepted as the highest authority. Principles of धर्म are deeply hidden. Hence that alone is the way which great men tread.
*
The यक्ष who was actually यम-धर्म, the god of death, was immensely pleased by these answers. He not only revived all the dead brothers of युधिष्ठिर but also gave him other boons asked by him.
